outline.chapter_title: FOIA Fundamentals: Structure, Purpose, and Litigation Posture
outline.description: Introduces the Freedom of Information Act, the request–response framework, agency obligations, and how FOIA disputes are litigated and reviewed.
subtopics: FOIA’s core mandate: disclosure as the rule, exemptions as the exception
Statutory framework: 5 U.S.C. § 552(a) (requests, timing, appeals) and § 552(b) (exemptions)
Agency duties: search adequacy, processing deadlines, and administrative appeal
Burden of proof on the government and the de novo standard of judicial review
Summary judgment as the typical vehicle in FOIA cases
The role of agency declarations and Vaughn indices in building the record
Where segregability fits in every FOIA case

outline.chapter_title: The Law Enforcement Exemptions: Exemption 7 in Context
outline.description: Provides an overview of Exemption 7 and its six subparts, situating Exemption 7(A) among other law-enforcement-related protections.
subtopics: Threshold requirement: records compiled for law enforcement purposes
Subparts overview: 7(A) through 7(F) and distinct harms each targets
Relationship between Exemption 7 and other exemptions (e.g., 1 and 3) in national security cases
Supreme Court validation of categorical approaches under 7(A): Robbins Tire & Rubber Co. v. NLRB
When agencies may rely on categorical rather than document-by-document showings

outline.chapter_title: “Compiled for Law Enforcement Purposes”: The Pratt–Campbell Standard
outline.description: Explains the threshold inquiry for all Exemption 7 claims, including the rational nexus requirement and differences between specialized and mixed-function agencies.
subtopics: Pratt v. Webster: rational nexus to agency’s law enforcement duties and a possible violation of federal law
Campbell v. DOJ and Clemente v. FBI: deference to the FBI as a specialized law enforcement agency
What counts as compilation for law enforcement purposes (including counterterrorism and intelligence-driven investigations)
Applying the threshold in practice: articulating the individual/incident connection to security risks
Using public and ex parte details to establish the threshold without compromising investigations

outline.chapter_title: Exemption 7(A): Interference with Pending or Reasonably Anticipated Enforcement Proceedings
outline.description: Develops the doctrine governing Exemption 7(A), emphasizing the requirement that proceedings be pending or reasonably anticipated and the kinds of interference that justify withholding.
subtopics: Text and burden: “could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings”
Defining “enforcement proceedings”: criminal, civil, and administrative; ongoing investigations as proceedings
Citizens for Responsibility & Ethics in Washington (CREW) v. DOJ and Juarez v. DOJ: proving pending or reasonably anticipated proceedings
Types of cognizable interference: tipping off targets, revealing scope and strategy, chilling witnesses
Time and staleness: how passage of time affects the showing; when updates are needed
Categorical withholding authorized under Robbins Tire and how to define defensible categories

outline.chapter_title: Proving and Policing 7(A): Affidavits, Vaughn Indices, and Ex Parte/In Camera Practice
outline.description: Explores the evidentiary tools courts accept for Exemption 7(A), including when ex parte submissions are permissible and how specific affidavits must be.
subtopics: Vaughn v. Rosen requirements and the adequacy of categorical descriptions
Levels of specificity: sufficient detail without compromising the investigation
Use of ex parte and in camera submissions: necessity, limits, and fairness concerns
Deference in national security contexts (CNSS) and how it affects affidavit sufficiency
Handling “vague” or conclusory submissions and the need for updates when delays occur
Refreshing the record: addressing staleness with supplemental declarations

outline.chapter_title: Segregability: The Statutory Duty to Release Nonexempt Material
outline.description: Details the requirement that agencies take reasonable steps to segregate and release nonexempt information, and the standards courts apply to assess compliance.
subtopics: Statutory language: 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and § 552(b) mandates
Meaningful information versus isolated words: Mead Data Center’s “inextricably intertwined” concept
When categorical withholdings defeat segregability and when they don’t
Perioperative Services & Logistics LLC v. VA: reliance on ex parte submissions to decide segregability
Practical indicators of non-segregability in law enforcement/national security files
Judicial tools: in camera review, sampling, and requiring granular justifications

outline.chapter_title: National Security, Counterterrorism, and Deference under FOIA
outline.description: Examines how national security considerations shape Exemption 7(A) analysis, including enhanced deference, the mosaic theory, and interactions with other exemptions.
subtopics: CNSS v. DOJ: consistent deference to the Executive in FOIA when national security is implicated
Mosaic concerns: how seemingly innocuous details can reveal sensitive operations
Choice of exemptions: why agencies sometimes rely on 7(A) rather than 1 or 3
Parallel proceedings and collateral forums (e.g., immigration removal) affecting FOIA justifications
Public-source information versus official confirmation risks

outline.description: Covers the procedural building blocks: exhaustion, summary judgment, standard of review, forfeiture, and strategic motion practice.
subtopics: Exhaustion and timing: when a requester may sue
Summary judgment in FOIA: record-based resolution via declarations
Appellate review: de novo standard and deference to agency expertise where appropriate
Forfeiture and issue preservation: raising challenges to categories and segregability (Khine v. DHS; Gallant v. NLRB)
Protective orders, sealed filings, and structuring the record to permit meaningful review
Remedies and remands: when courts order refreshed or more detailed submissions

outline.chapter_title: Case Study: Farahi v. FBI as a Vehicle for Exemption 7(A)
outline.description: Uses Farahi as a structured teaching case to illustrate the elements and evidentiary showings required under Exemption 7(A), including the role of supplemental declarations and segregability findings.
subtopics: Factual background: FOIA request for FBI file, immigration context, and counterterrorism allegations
The record: initial Hardy declarations (public and ex parte), district court’s staleness concern, and Bender’s updates
Threshold met: compiled for law enforcement purposes under Pratt/Campbell
Pending or reasonably anticipated proceedings: combining public and ex parte detail; addressing CREW’s caution on vagueness
Interference rationale: tipping off targets and revealing scope of ongoing investigations
Categorical withholdings and the requester’s forfeiture of category-specific challenges
Segregability: reliance on ex parte submissions and the “meaningful information” standard
Appellate posture: de novo review, deference in national security, and affirmance

outline.chapter_title: Comparative Doctrine: Positioning Farahi Among Leading Cases
outline.description: Places Farahi alongside seminal decisions to highlight continuity and nuance in Exemption 7(A) doctrine.
subtopics: Robbins Tire: Supreme Court’s approval of categorical 7(A) withholdings during active enforcement
CREW v. DOJ: defining “pending or reasonably anticipated” and policing conclusory affidavits
Juarez v. DOJ: ongoing investigations as proceedings and the harm of premature release
Pratt, Campbell, Clemente: establishing law enforcement purpose and judicial deference to the FBI
Mead Data and Perioperative Services: segregability’s limits and ex parte reliance
Gallant and category specificity: how to craft categories that survive judicial scrutiny

outline.chapter_title: Practitioner’s Toolkit: Litigating and Resisting 7(A) Claims
outline.description: Offers practical guidance for requesters and agencies on building or challenging Exemption 7(A) withholdings, including strategies related to staleness, categories, and segregability.
subtopics: Requester strategies: demanding specificity, attacking overbroad categories, and leveraging staleness for updates
Agency strategies: drafting detailed but non-prejudicial declarations and using categorical Vaughn submissions
When and how to seek or oppose ex parte/in camera review
Framing segregability: demonstrating “inextricably intertwined” records versus proposing practical redaction regimes
Preserving issues: avoiding forfeiture of category-based objections and segregability challenges
Anticipating collateral proceedings (criminal, administrative, immigration) that bear on 7(A)

outline.description: Analyzes Farahi’s contribution to Exemption 7(A), especially in long-running national security investigations and the use of supplemental declarations to address staleness.
subtopics: Reaffirmation of robust deference to the FBI in counterterrorism contexts
Operational lesson: updating declarations can cure staleness without re-litigating the entire record
Validation of ex parte submissions for both interference and segregability showings
Boundaries of CREW’s vagueness concerns: contextual readings of terse updates
Practical consequence: sustained viability of categorical 7(A) withholdings in complex, multi-decade investigations
Open questions: interplay with the FOIA Improvement Act’s foreseeable harm provision and the threshold for requiring more public detail
